nameStory: Rough Thelia gets its common name from its distinctly rough, scratchy texture when you run your fingers across it. The word 'thelia' comes from the Greek word meaning 'nipple' or 'teat,' referring to the small, rounded bumps that give this moss its characteristic roughness.
description: Rough Thelia is a small, creeping moss that forms loose, irregular mats on tree bark and rocks. It grows in thin, branching patterns that look almost feathery, rarely getting more than an inch tall. The tiny leaves overlap like shingles on a roof, creating a somewhat flattened appearance. When dry, it becomes quite brittle and rough to the touch, but softens considerably when moist.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Distinctly rough and scratchy when you gently stroke it with your finger - much rougher than most other small mosses

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, irregular mats that creep across surfaces in branching, feathery patterns rather than dense cushions

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves overlap tightly like roof shingles, creating a flattened appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dull green to yellowish-green when moist, becoming brownish and almost bronze-colored when dry

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on tree bark, especially on the lower trunks of deciduous trees

habitat: Rough Thelia is typically found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly maples, oaks, and birches in mixed forests throughout New England. It prefers the lower portions of tree trunks where humidity stays higher, often on the north-facing sides. You'll occasionally spot it on wooden fences or other weathered wood surfaces in wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring rains hydrate the moss, making it softer and easier to identify by texture.
seasonality.summer: May appear brownish and very rough during dry spells, but maintains its characteristic scratchy feel even when dehydrated.
seasonality.fall: Often most noticeable in fall when leaves drop and expose more tree bark, showing bronze to brown coloration.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but appears quite brittle and rough, with a distinctive brownish winter color.

funFact: Despite being called 'rough,' this moss becomes surprisingly soft and almost velvety when thoroughly soaked - it can absorb up to 20 times its dry weight in water, completely transforming its texture in minutes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Common Thelia, but Rough Thelia lives up to its name - it's noticeably scratchier to the touch. Memory trick: 'Rough Thelia is truly rough' - if it doesn't feel distinctly scratchy, it's probably the common species.
compareHints: Rough Thelia is much more abrasive to the touch than its relative Common Thelia, which feels relatively smooth when you stroke it gently. While both species form similar feathery, creeping mats on tree bark, Rough Thelia also tends to have a more bronze or yellowish cast to its coloration. The roughness difference is so pronounced that you can often identify Rough Thelia by touch alone, even with your eyes closed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Thelia differs from Rough Thelia primarily in its smoother texture and more regular branching pattern – Rough Thelia feels distinctly rougher to the touch and has a more chaotic growth form.
